title: Quick Ceasefire Limits Damage
description: The conflict ends within weeks through a Turkey-mediated ceasefire, limiting humanitarian damage to what has already occurred plus a brief wind-down period. The death toll stabilizes near 2,000-2,500 as strikes cease. The 24,800+ injured receive improved care as humanitarian access opens rapidly post-ceasefire. Infrastructure destruction is extensive but not catastrophic — the energy-strike pause holds, preserving Iran's oil and gas infrastructure for post-war reconstruction revenue. GCC food crisis eases within weeks as Hormuz reopens under escort. Refugee displacement stays under 500k as the ceasefire removes the primary push factor. Iran's public health system is strained but does not collapse, as international medical teams gain access. Environmental damage remains moderate. This is the best achievable humanitarian outcome from the current position — the damage already done (1,937 killed, 24,800+ injured, 120+ cultural sites, 11,000+ strikes) cannot be undone, but further escalation is prevented.

title: Grinding War of Attrition
description: The conflict extends for months without decisive military or diplomatic resolution. The US air campaign continues, expanding target sets as priority military targets are exhausted. Civilian casualties climb steadily — averaging 50-70 deaths per day, pushing the toll past 5,000 within two months and potentially toward 10,000 by mid-2026. The 24,800+ injured figure doubles as the healthcare system's capacity degrades from infrastructure damage and supply chain disruption. Chronic disease patients begin dying from treatment interruption: dialysis patients, cancer patients on chemotherapy, diabetics dependent on insulin cold chain. Displacement accelerates as entire urban neighborhoods become uninhabitable — the 100k-500k figure grows toward 1-2 million. Iran's remaining command structure hardens into a resistance posture. The GCC food crisis deepens as Hormuz remains closed. Environmental damage accumulates from industrial facility strikes. War crimes allegations intensify as international media documents the mounting civilian toll. This is the Iran-Iraq War model: intense enough to cause enormous suffering but without the dramatic escalation that forces international intervention.

title: Humanitarian Catastrophe
description: Infrastructure collapse triggers cascading civilian crisis far exceeding direct strike casualties. After the April 6 deadline, US strikes on energy infrastructure disable Iran's electrical grid within weeks. Without electricity, water pumping stations fail within 72 hours in most cities. Hospital backup generators exhaust fuel supplies within days. The cascading effects unfold rapidly: waterborne disease outbreaks (cholera, typhoid) emerge in displaced populations; neonatal mortality spikes; cold chain collapse spoils insulin and vaccines; food spoilage accelerates. This pattern was documented in Iraq 1991 — post-Desert Storm infrastructure destruction killed an estimated 100,000-500,000 children under 5 from disease over the following decade (UNICEF). The death toll accelerates past 10,000 within months, primarily from secondary health effects rather than direct strikes. Displacement becomes mass exodus: 2M+ flee toward Turkey, Iraq, Pakistan. The GCC food crisis becomes famine risk as Hormuz stays closed and regional logistics collapse. Aid access is effectively blocked by ongoing operations and infrastructure destruction. The ICC opens a formal investigation. This becomes the defining humanitarian disaster of the 2020s.

title: Nuclear/Chemical Contamination
description: Strikes on Iranian nuclear or industrial facilities cause radiological or chemical contamination, creating an environmental disaster with generational health consequences. Iran's nuclear facilities (Natanz, Fordow, Isfahan, Bushehr) and petrochemical complexes (Asaluyeh, Mahshahr) contain materials that, if dispersed by military strikes, could contaminate large areas. The Bushehr nuclear power plant, containing spent fuel rods, poses the highest risk — a strike causing fuel rod dispersal would create a Fukushima-scale contamination event in the Persian Gulf. Even non-nuclear industrial facilities contain hazardous materials: petrochemical plants, chemical storage, and enrichment byproducts. The contamination plume from Isfahan's UCF facility (containing UF6 stockpiles) could affect populations downwind for hundreds of kilometers. This scenario transforms the humanitarian crisis from a conventional war emergency into a multi-decade environmental disaster. Contaminated zones become permanently uninhabitable. Cancer rates spike in affected populations over 10-30 years. The Persian Gulf marine ecosystem faces catastrophic damage. This is the tail risk that distinguishes this conflict from conventional wars.
